title: Iran Signals Wider Targets and New Tactics if War With US and Israel Resumes
excerpt: Tehran says its forces are stronger and on higher alert, names undersea cables, data centres and energy sites as potential targets, and insists the Strait of Hormuz stays closed — while Qatari mediation continues.
body:
• Iran's army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said on Saturday its forces are "on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war" with the United States and Israel, and that any response ordered by the Supreme Leader would be "immediate, effective and without geographical limitations."
  • Tehran is signalling a wider target set if fighting resumes: IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said new, previously unattacked targets have been identified, and Iranian officials have pointed to undersea communications cables, data centres and energy facilities in the Gulf.
  • Iran says the Strait of Hormuz — which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption — will stay closed until Washington meets its demands, a direct risk to fuel prices and import bills for oil-importing countries including India.
  • The warnings are deterrence signalling, not a decision to restart the war: mediators including Qatar are still working to prevent a resumption of fighting, and US President Donald Trump called Qatar's Emir on Friday to discuss ending the war.

Iran is preparing for the possibility that its war with the United States and Israel resumes, and it is using a series of public statements to signal that a second round would look different from the first: a broader target list, revised tactics around the Strait of Hormuz, and a response its commanders say would not be confined by geography.

On Saturday, Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said the country's armed forces are "on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war," having gained experience from direct confrontation with US and Israeli forces. "Under the order of the Supreme Leader, the response of the armed forces will be immediate, effective and without geographical limitations," he told the official IRNA news agency, in remarks reported by Hatha Alyoum.

A wider list of targets

The clearest change in Tehran's messaging is the range of targets it is now naming. Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Hossein Mohebbi has said Iran has identified new targets that have not previously been attacked, and Iranian security officials have warned that a future response could extend beyond military bases to infrastructure that supports the region's economy.

Two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters in October that Tehran had developed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel resumed large-scale attacks, and that Iran could also seek to delay repairs, according to an NBC News account of the preparations synthesised by The Fox Daily. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei has warned that digital infrastructure and energy facilities could be targeted, and the reported target set includes data centres and artificial intelligence facilities linked to American technology companies, oil and gas installations, and military and naval facilities across the region.

These are warnings and stated intentions, not evidence that Iran could successfully strike every target it has named. Their purpose is deterrent: to raise the expected cost of another US-Israeli campaign by putting the Gulf's energy, finance and technology infrastructure inside the frame.

New tactics in the Strait of Hormuz

The strait remains the centre of Iran's leverage. Akraminia said Tehran retained control over the waterway and that it would remain closed until Washington met Iran's demands. The strait normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption, so any sustained closure feeds directly into fuel prices in importing countries, including India.

Iranian officials told Reuters in October that the country had changed its tactics against vessels it considered to be violating its restrictions, altering the type and frequency of attacks. A US military official said Iranian forces had begun using small boats carrying unarmed spotters to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels — a change that reportedly followed damage to much of Iran's coastal radar network during American strikes.

On November 7, the Revolutionary Guard also announced it had lifted its previously stated self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres on ballistic missile range. Mohebbi told the Fars news agency that "the increase in the range of Iran's missiles continues steadily." The announcement changes Iran's public messaging about its capabilities; it does not by itself establish the operational range of any deployed missile.

Diplomacy has not stopped

The military signalling is running alongside active mediation. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had held calls with counterparts from 12 countries over the past 48 hours, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkey, Egypt, Iraq and Pakistan, stressing what he called Iran's right to defend its sovereignty and calling for regional security arrangements without outside interference.

On the American side, President Donald Trump called Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani on Friday to discuss efforts to end the war. On Friday, the US military also offered a $20 million reward, and possible relocation, for information on Iran's nuclear programme — a reminder that the nuclear dispute at the heart of the conflict remains unresolved. Early on Saturday, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with no official assessment of damage immediately available.

What to watch

Preparations and threats are not the same as a decision to restart the war, and mediators are still working to prevent exactly that. What has changed is the shape of Tehran's deterrence: a public claim of greater strength, an explicitly expanded target list, missile-range messaging, and tactical adaptation in the strait. For readers in India and the diaspora, the most direct exposure runs through the Hormuz closure itself — energy shipments, shipping costs and the fuel prices that follow from both.
